paragraphs.text: Deep inside limestone caves in parts of Europe, Asia and elsewhere, far beyond the reach of daylight, are some of the oldest images ever made by human beings: horses, bison, deer and other animals painted in red and black on the rock, together with hand stencils, dots and lines whose meaning is unknown. Some caves contain hundreds of images; others hold only a few. When the most famous of these caves were first reported in the late nineteenth century, many experts refused to believe that such skilful work could be the product of prehistoric people, and some accused the discoverers of forgery. It took decades, and the discovery of many more decorated caves, before the great age of the paintings was generally accepted.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Dating the paintings has always been difficult. The pigments are mostly minerals, such as red iron oxides, which cannot be dated directly, and only images made with charcoal contain the carbon needed for radiocarbon dating. Even then, the date shows when the wood was burned, not necessarily when it was used, and the tiny samples required can damage the painting, and contamination by later carbon is a further hazard. For much of the twentieth century, researchers therefore relied on style, placing images in a sequence from simple to sophisticated on the assumption that art had developed gradually. Radiocarbon results from the 1990s onwards overturned that assumption: some of the most accomplished paintings turned out to be among the oldest.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: A newer method has changed the picture again. In many caves, water seeping through the rock leaves thin layers of mineral crust over the paintings. These crusts contain tiny amounts of uranium, which decays at a known rate, so measuring the products of that decay shows when the crust formed. Because the crust lies on top of the paint, the painting must be older than the crust, which gives a minimum age rather than an exact date. Using this technique, researchers have dated hand stencils and animal figures in caves in Spain and in Southeast Asia to more than forty thousand years ago, far earlier than many had expected. Some results remain disputed, however, since water can wash uranium out of a crust and make it appear older than it really is.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: How the paintings were made is better understood. Experiments by archaeologists have shown that red and black pigments were ground into powder and mixed with water or with animal fat, and then applied with fingers, pads of moss or fur, or brushes made from hair. Some pigment was blown onto the wall through a hollow bone or directly from the mouth, which is how many of the hand stencils were produced: a hand was pressed against the rock and paint sprayed around it. Stone lamps burning animal fat have been found in several caves, and tests show that they gave a steady, smoky light, bright enough to work by but far dimmer than daylight. Scaffolding, or at least ledges of rock, must have been used to reach the highest images.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The question of why people went to such trouble is much harder to answer, since the painters left no explanation. Early interpretations treated the images as hunting magic, intended to ensure success in the hunt, but studies of animal bones found at nearby sites showed that the species most often painted were not always those most often eaten. Other researchers have suggested that the caves were places of ritual, that the images record stories, or that they mark territory. Studies of the acoustics of some caves found that paintings are concentrated in places where sound echoes most strongly, which suggests that sound as well as sight may have been part of the experience. None of these ideas excludes the others, and the purpose may have changed over the thousands of years during which the caves were used.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: The hand stencils have attracted particular attention because they seem to offer a direct trace of individual people. By measuring the relative length of the fingers, which differs on average between men and women, some researchers have concluded that a large proportion of the stencils were made by women, contradicting the long-held assumption that cave painters were mostly adult men. The method is contested, since the difference between the sexes is small and varies between populations, but it has encouraged archaeologists to question who took part in making the images. Small hand stencils placed high on walls suggest that children were sometimes present and were lifted up to add their marks.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The caves themselves are now at risk from the attention they receive. After one of the best-known sites opened to the public in the mid-twentieth century, the breath and body heat of hundreds of thousands of visitors changed the air inside, and green algae and later mould began to grow on the walls. The cave was closed, and visitors today see an exact replica built nearby, so precise that even the bumps of the rock have been copied. Similar replicas have since been made for other sites, and some archaeologists argue that they allow the public to experience the art without contributing to its destruction, while others feel that a copy, however faithful, cannot convey what it means to stand in the original darkness.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The pawnshop is one of the oldest financial institutions in the world, and one of the least respected. Its principle is simple. A customer brings an object of value, such as a watch, a piece of jewellery or a musical instrument, and receives a loan for a fraction of what it is worth. If the loan and a fee are repaid within an agreed period, the object is returned; if not, the lender keeps it and sells it. The fee is usually a fixed percentage of the loan for each month it is outstanding, and most pledged items are eventually reclaimed. No questions are asked about the borrower’s income or history, because the object itself is the lender’s security. For people with nothing else to offer, that simplicity has always been the attraction.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Lending against goods is recorded in ancient China, where pawnshops existed as early as the fifth century, and in the Roman world. In medieval Europe, however, lending at interest was widely condemned, and pawnbroking was often left to groups excluded from other trades, which added to its poor reputation. In the fifteenth century, charitable foundations in Italian cities responded to the high interest charged by private lenders by setting up public pawn banks, which lent to the poor at low rates and used any surplus for good works. Some of these institutions later developed into ordinary savings banks, and several still exist. Their example was copied in other countries, often with the support of city governments.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: In the industrial cities of the nineteenth century, the pawnshop became part of the weekly rhythm of working-class life. Many families pawned their best clothes on Monday, when money had run out, and redeemed them on Saturday after wages were paid, so that they could be worn on Sunday. Surveys carried out at the time found that in some poor districts almost every household used a pawnbroker regularly, and that the same items might pass back and forth across the counter dozens of times a year. Pawnbrokers in such districts knew their customers well and could often judge an item’s value at a glance. For such families the pawnshop was less a last resort than a way of managing an income that arrived weekly and ran out before the end of the week. The pawnshop, in other words, served as a bank for people whom banks ignored.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Critics at the time and since have pointed to the cost of this kind of borrowing. Although the fee on a single short loan looks small, when it is expressed as an annual rate it can be very high, and customers who fail to redeem an item lose it for far less than its value. Some reformers wanted pawnshops abolished altogether. Others in several countries campaigned for regulation, and laws introduced from the late nineteenth century onwards set maximum rates, required pawnbrokers to keep records and give receipts, and obliged them to return any surplus to the customer when an unredeemed item was sold for more than the debt. Enforcement was uneven, however, and complaints about unfair valuations continued well into the twentieth century.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Defenders of pawnbroking argue that its costs must be compared with the alternatives available to its customers rather than with the rates charged by banks. A pawn loan cannot lead to an ever-growing debt, since the most a borrower can lose is the object pledged, and it does not affect a credit record. The economist Elena Ruiz has shown that when cheap public pawn lending was withdrawn in some places, many former customers turned not to banks, which would not lend to them, but to informal lenders who charged more and used threats to collect their money. Ruiz does not claim that pawn loans are cheap, only that for many borrowers the realistic choice lies elsewhere than a bank.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: In the second half of the twentieth century pawnshops declined in many rich countries, as rising wages, consumer credit and credit cards gave most households other ways to borrow. They did not disappear, however, and in several countries they have grown again since the financial crisis of 2008, when banks became more cautious about lending to people with low incomes. Modern pawnshops often look very different from their predecessors, with bright shopfronts and online valuations, and many now earn more from selling second-hand goods than from lending. Some have also added services such as cheque cashing and small personal loans.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: In much of the world pawnbroking remains a mainstream form of credit. In parts of Asia and Latin America, pawnshops are large businesses, some owned or regulated by the state, and gold jewellery, which many families hold partly as savings, is the most commonly pledged item. In some places a wedding or a school fee is commonly financed in this way. Researchers studying these markets note that a rise in the price of gold allows households to borrow more against the same jewellery, so that pawnshop lending tends to grow when gold is expensive. For the people who use them, pawnshops continue to offer what they always have: money quickly, without paperwork, in exchange for something they can hope to get back. Few institutions have changed so little in so long.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: Every autumn, in many countries, the shortlists for major book prizes are announced, and for a few weeks the novels on them are reviewed, displayed and argued about. For the winners, the effect can be dramatic: a book that had sold a few thousand copies may sell hundreds of thousands in the months after the award. Publishers plan their autumn lists with the prize season in mind, and in some countries the ceremony is broadcast live on television. Prizes have multiplied over the past half-century, and there are now awards for first novels, for translated fiction, for crime, for poetry and for non-fiction. It seems a good moment to ask whether they do what they claim to do, which is to direct readers towards the best new writing. The question is not new, but the answers have changed as the prizes have grown.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The case for prizes is strongest when it is made on behalf of books that would otherwise go unnoticed. Most new novels sell very few copies, and bookshops and newspapers have limited space, and a new novel by an unknown author may be reviewed nowhere at all. The publishing researcher Nadia Kareem, who has tracked the sales of shortlisted books over two decades, found that the benefit of a place on a shortlist was greatest for books from small publishers and by authors with no previous success; established names gained comparatively little. In her view, prizes act as a kind of public filter that gives unknown writers a chance to be discovered. She notes, too, that the effect lasts: shortlisted authors are more likely to find a publisher for their next book.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Critics reply that the filter is not as neutral as it appears. Judges are usually writers, critics or academics, and are rarely chosen from the general public. The judges of most prizes are few in number, usually five or fewer, and change every year, so a different panel might easily have chosen a different winner. The sociologist Paul Brennan, who has studied the backgrounds of judges, argues that panels tend to reward a narrow range of serious literary fiction and to overlook genres such as crime or science fiction, however well written. Prizes, he suggests, do not so much identify quality as reproduce the tastes of a small group of people who share a similar education and experience. He does not accuse judges of bad faith, only of sharing assumptions they rarely examine.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: I think Brennan overstates the point. Taste is always personal, and a single reviewer in a newspaper has no greater claim to neutrality than a panel of five, and it is not obvious what neutrality would even mean in judging a novel. The fact that different judges would choose differently is not an argument against prizes but a reason for having many of them, each with its own criteria. The growth of specialist awards over recent decades, for genres and forms that the major prizes ignored, seems to me a healthy response to exactly the problem he identifies. Readers who dislike the choices of one prize can simply follow another.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: A more serious concern is what prizes do to the books that do not win. Because the winner receives most of the attention, sales are concentrated on a very small number of titles, and bookshops increasingly stock shortlisted books at the expense of others. Shortlisted titles occupy the tables near the entrance, while other new novels are placed on the shelves further inside. The economist Lena Fischer has found that in the weeks after a major award, sales of fiction as a whole do not rise; readers buy the winner instead of, rather than in addition to, other novels. If she is right, prizes change what people read without making them read more. Fischer’s data cover only a few years, and she accepts that the pattern might differ elsewhere.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: There is also the question of what winning does to writers. Interviews, festivals and travel can leave little time for writing. Some authors have described the pressure that followed a major prize, when a quiet career suddenly became a public one and every subsequent book was compared with the prize-winner. The literary historian Samuel Okoro points out that a surprising number of winners of the most prestigious awards published little of significance afterwards, although he is careful to say that this may reflect nothing more than the difficulty of repeating an exceptional achievement. Several winners have said that the prize changed their lives for the better.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: On balance, I think prizes do more good than harm, but only if readers treat them as a starting point rather than a verdict. A shortlist is a set of recommendations made by a few people with particular tastes, and it is most useful to readers who know that. Treated as the final word on quality, it can do harm. The danger lies not in the prizes themselves but in the habit of reading only what has already been chosen by someone else. A reader who picks up a shortlisted novel and then goes on to explore the books around it on the shelf has used a prize well. Prizes can open a door; it is up to readers to walk further in.
paragraphs.label: G

topic.en: Three texts: how cave paintings are dated and studied, the history of the pawnshop, and the argument about whether literary prizes help readers.

explanation.ru: Абзац E: заёмщик может потерять лишь заложенную вещь → E. В D говорится о высокой стоимости займа — это довод критиков, а не объяснение пределов долга.

items.quote: when banks became more cautious about lending to people with low incomes
items.prompt: a reason for the recent revival of pawnshops in some wealthy countries

explanation.en: Paragraph F: after 2008 banks became cautious about low-income borrowers → F.
explanation.kk: F абзацы: 2008 жылғы дағдарыстан кейін банктер табысы аз адамдарға сақтықпен қарады → F.
explanation.ru: Абзац F: после кризиса 2008 года банки стали осторожнее с малообеспеченными → F.

items.quote: pawnbroking was often left to groups excluded from other trades
items.prompt: a mention of people shut out of other occupations taking up the business

explanation.en: Paragraph B: pawnbroking was left to groups excluded from other trades → B.
explanation.kk: B абзацы: пайызбен қарыз беру айыпталған, ломбард басқа кәсіпке жіберілмеген топтарға қалған → B.
explanation.ru: Абзац B: ростовщичество осуждали, и ломбарды оставляли группам, которых не пускали в другие ремёсла → B.

groups.instruction: Text 2 has seven paragraphs, A–G. Which paragraph contains the following information? Write the correct letter, A–G.

items.quote: Prizes have multiplied over the past half-century
items.prompt: There are far more book awards than there were fifty years ago.

explanation.en: “Prizes have multiplied over the past half-century” → YES.
explanation.kk: «Prizes have multiplied over the past half-century» → YES.
explanation.ru: «Prizes have multiplied over the past half-century» → YES.

items.quote: the benefit of a place on a shortlist was greatest for books from small publishers
items.prompt: Most shortlisted novels are published by small firms.

explanation.en: Small publishers benefit most, but their share of shortlists is never given → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.kk: Шағын баспалардың кітабына шорт-лист көбірек көмектесетіні айтылған, бірақ олардың шорт-листтегі үлесі айтылмаған → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.ru: Сказано, что книгам малых издательств шорт-лист помогает сильнее всего, но какая доля шорт-листа у них, не сказано → NOT GIVEN.

items.quote: is not an argument against prizes but a reason for having many of them
items.prompt: Disagreement between panels of judges is a good reason to do away with prizes.

explanation.en: “not an argument against prizes but a reason for having many of them” → NO.
explanation.kk: «not an argument against prizes but a reason for having many of them» → NO.
explanation.ru: «not an argument against prizes but a reason for having many of them» → NO.

items.quote: The growth of specialist awards over recent decades
items.prompt: Specialist awards now attract bigger audiences than the major prizes.

explanation.en: The writer welcomes specialist awards but says nothing about their audiences → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.kk: Автор арнайы сыйлықтардың көбеюін құптайды, бірақ олардың аудиториясы туралы айтпайды → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.ru: Автор одобряет рост специализированных премий, но об их аудитории ничего не говорит → NOT GIVEN.

items.quote: bookshops increasingly stock shortlisted books at the expense of others
items.prompt: Bookshops keep shortlisted titles on display for longer than they once did.

explanation.en: Shops increasingly stock shortlisted titles, but display time is not mentioned → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.kk: Дүкендер шорт-листтегі кітапты басқалардың орнына жиі ұстайтыны айтылған; көрсету мерзімі айтылмаған → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.ru: Сказано, что магазины всё чаще держат книги из шорт-листа вместо других; о сроках показа — ничего → NOT GIVEN.

items.quote: it is most useful to readers who know that
items.prompt: A shortlist is most useful to readers who understand how it was chosen.

explanation.en: A shortlist reflects particular tastes and is “most useful to readers who know that” → YES.
explanation.kk: Шорт-лист — өз талғамы бар аз адамның ұсынысы, «most useful to readers who know that» → YES.
explanation.ru: Шорт-лист — рекомендации немногих людей со своими вкусами, «most useful to readers who know that» → YES.

groups.instruction: Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer in Text 3? Write YES if the statement agrees with the claims of the writer, NO if the statement contradicts the claims of the writer, NOT GIVEN if it is impossible to say what the writer thinks about this.

items.quote: published little of significance afterwards
items.prompt: Winning a major award may be followed by a fall in an author’s output.

explanation.en: Okoro: many winners published little of significance afterwards → D.
explanation.kk: Okoro: көп лауреат кейін маңызды ештеңе шығармаған → D.
explanation.ru: Okoro: многие лауреаты потом почти ничего значимого не издали → D.

items.quote: panels tend to reward a narrow range of serious literary fiction
items.prompt: Judges tend to favour one particular type of writing.

explanation.en: Brennan: panels reward a narrow range of literary fiction → B.
explanation.kk: Brennan: қазылар алқасы тар шеңбердегі байсалды прозаны марапаттап, жанрларды елемейді → B.
explanation.ru: Brennan: жюри награждает узкий круг серьёзной прозы и не замечает жанры → B.

items.quote: readers buy the winner instead of, rather than in addition to, other novels
items.prompt: Prizes shift readers’ choices without increasing the amount they read.

explanation.en: Fischer: readers buy the winner instead of other novels, so total sales do not rise → C.
explanation.kk: Fischer: сыйлықтан кейін проза сатылымы өспейді, жеңімпазды басқа кітаптың орнына алады → C.
explanation.ru: Fischer: после премии продажи прозы в целом не растут, покупают победителя вместо других книг → C. Вывод «change what people read without making them read more» делает автор из её данных.

items.quote: by authors with no previous success; established names gained comparatively little
items.prompt: Unknown writers gain most from appearing on a shortlist.

explanation.en: Kareem: authors with no previous success gain most → A.
explanation.kk: Kareem: бұрын табысқа жетпеген авторлар көп ұтады, танымалдар аз → A.
explanation.ru: Kareem: больше всего выигрывают авторы без прежнего успеха, известные — мало → A.
